text: As many of us spin back up our recruiting efforts in Q1, a caution in SaaS that the #1 most common misfire is the VP/head of sales. Because in SaaS start-ups, it seems like the majority of first VP Sales fail. Don’t even make it 12 months. And totally screw things up as they fail. And this is really, really painful. It’s much worse than a bad VP Marketing hire. Because with a bad VP of Sales, you can lose so much momentum and create so much internal confusion that this bad hire can cripple you as you try to get from Initial Traction to Initial Scale. So I want to try to help you if you’re going through this.

Vibe Coding, Day 81: I've now got 7 pretty bitchin' apps into production on Replit. That's just so cool. But I screwed the first one up and never got it out, after 100+ hours. Here are The Top 10 Mistakes I Made: Mistake #1: Starting Off With Too Complex an App A number of folks warned me on this, but I decided to go all-in on vibe-coded App #1. I decided to push the limits, knowingly. But my mistake wasn't knowing the limits before I pushed them. I started off with way too complex an app that attempted to dynamically match 10,000+ execs with each other, on the fly. This was dumb. First, I should have done it with AI (see point 4). But beyond that, I should have Started Simple. Mistake #2: Trusting the AI Agent. Yes "Trust" — But Verify. 90% of my struggling with my first vibe coded app was trusting the AI Agent too much. Many pointed this out as I struggled, but my point was -- I Should Be Able to Trust the Agent. Here's the thing. You have to learn the tools. They aren't perfect. They, in their own way, do "hallucinate". They make things up. Mistake #3: Building Anything I Didn’t 100% Understand Ok this wrecked my first app and almost wrecked me several times since. Just because you can spec out an app and write up a PRD, it doesn't mean you will >understand< how it works. Especially if you aren't a developer. Several times, I've in essence used the AI Agent to build a complex algorithm. Don't Do This. IMHE at least.

text: Buddy, I have been looking at a lot of pitches from founders over the last week or two, and some of them truly are amazing. Some of them just leap off the page, and you just want to meet with that founder right then and there, but typically you see a bell-shaped distribution. Um, a handful of pitches really leap off the page. A bunch are are are terrible, are simply terrible, and most are in the middle. Most are have something interesting. There's there's some hint. There's something in the email, in the subject line, in the deck that's interesting, but it's not as interesting as it could be. And I want to talk about that because there's no reason if you're pitching investors that your pitch should be in the middle of the bell curve. It should be as good as it possibly can be. And I wanted to review 16 rookie errors that I see founders make again and again when pitch investors where there's no need, no need to make these mistakes. And if you fix these mistakes, if you don't make them, you're going to go up that distribution. and you're going to be in that top 10% of pitches where folks really want to meet with you. The first one, it's really a combination of two points, which is that cold emails work, but they have to be awesome. And we recently did the new new venture at Saster. Um a little while ago we had some top VCs uh Ailen Lee from Cowboy, Keith Ra Boy, David Saxs, Kristoff Jance, um uh the the Forbes Midas list, uh three of the top VCs in the world, they all came and shared their learnings and you can see them on on YouTube on new venture.com. Um and what was interesting is the the ones that I interviewed, the top VCs that I talked to said they all read almost all the rebound emails. And this is contrary to many of the advice you get on the internet where you need a warm intro, you need to know the right people, you need to have gone to Stanford or being in the right accelerator and those things, there's no question that helps. Uh fair or not, discriminatory or not, um having social proof, having proof that you might be great helps. Um going to Stanford and Harvard helps. Graduating from out of Y Combinator helps, but the best VCs read their cold emails. So, so, so you're armed with that. you know that actually you can inbound to a top VC, at least seed VCs, at least early stage VCs, and they will probably read it. So, make it awesome, folks. It's a sales pitch. Folks don't want to hear um a oneline email about how you're better than Zoom. No, explain it. Make that subject line pop. Make the make every part of your pitch amazing. Have the email subject line be so awesome folks would want to um invest just off the subject line. Make the body of the email incredible, incredible. Share your best metrics, why you're going to win, why the team is great, why your vision is perfect. Distill it so that someone might invest just based on that email. And then if and then attach a deck and make that deck as awesome as it can be. Don't have a teaser deck. Don't throw off some random statistics about the market. Explain why someone should buy stock from you. Fundraising is selling stock. It is a specialized version of sales, but it is sales, no doubt. So, make the world's best email possible. And if you look below, I will share a link to two emails that I read, um, cold emails, and those companies are now worth literally, literally billions of dollars. These were pure cold emails to me that I funded for millions for companies that are now worth billions. It does happen. Does it happen every day? No. But nothing happens every day.
